passages.happening:
The sermons are over. Moses now speaks about himself. “I am now a hundred and twenty years old; I am no longer able to come and go, and the LORD has said to me, ‘You shall not cross the Jordan’” (verse 2).

He tells the people who will go with them in his place. “The LORD your God Himself will cross over ahead of you” (verse 3). Joshua will lead them. “Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid or terrified of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you; He will never leave you nor forsake you” (verse 6).

Then he calls Joshua forward and says it to him in front of everyone. “Be strong and courageous, for you will go with this people into the land” (verse 7). “The LORD Himself goes before you; He will be with you. He will never leave you nor forsake you. Do not be afraid or discouraged” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
For forty years Israel has known one leader. He brought them out of Egypt, stood between them and God at the mountain, and prayed for them when they deserved to be destroyed. Now he tells them he is leaving. A people could be forgiven for being afraid.

Notice the order of what he says. He does not begin with Joshua. He begins with God. ‘The LORD your God Himself will cross over ahead of you.’ The people are losing Moses. They are not losing the one who actually led them.

‘Be strong and courageous’ comes three times in this chapter. Moses says it to the people, then to Joshua, and God says it to Joshua in verse 23. It will be said again at the opening of the book of Joshua. The two Hebrew words mean to be firm and to be bold. The strength meant is not swagger. It is steadiness that rests on a promise: God goes with you.

The Hebrew word translated ‘forsake’ means to leave or abandon. God promises that he will not do it. Later in this chapter the same word is used of what Israel will do to God. The contrast is deliberate.

Moses commissions Joshua ‘in the presence of all Israel’. Leadership is handed over in public, so that no one can doubt it, and so that the people hear the promises on which Joshua will stand. An old leader gives his courage to a younger one.

The driving out of the nations in verses 3 to 5 belongs with chapter 7, and the note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out how Christians read it.
passages.later:
After Moses died, God said to Joshua what Moses had said: “As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Joshua 1:5).

The letter to the Hebrews gives the promise of verse 6 to every believer: ‘for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you”’ (Hebrews 13:5).

The last words of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel are the same promise in his own mouth: “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
passages.asks: Israel was losing the only leader it had known, and Moses pointed past himself. Ask whose presence you depend on so much that you cannot picture going on without it. Then hear verse 8. Ask who you could strengthen, in public and by name, for a task you are handing on.

passages.t: The law written down, and read to everyone
passages.happening:
“So Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel” (verse 9).

He commands a public reading. Every seven years, in the year when debts are released, at the Feast of Tabernacles, when all Israel comes before God at the place he chooses, ‘you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel’ (verses 10-11).

Everyone is to be there: men, women, children, and the foreigners who live in Israel's towns. They are to listen, ‘and learn to fear the LORD your God and to follow carefully all the words of this law’ (verse 12). “Then their children who do not know the law will listen and learn to fear the LORD your God” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Up to now the law has been spoken. Here it becomes a written text, which will outlast the man who spoke it.

Treaties of the ancient world often required that the written text be kept in a temple and read aloud to the people at fixed times. Deuteronomy follows that pattern. The resemblance helped Israel to understand its bond with God as a binding covenant with a king.

The time chosen for the reading says something. It was the seventh year, when debts were cancelled. And it was the Feast of Tabernacles, when the harvest was in and the whole nation was gathered, living in shelters to remember the wilderness. The people heard the law at the moment when they were freest and most thankful.

The audience is the whole people. Women are named. Children are named. Foreigners are named. In a world where few could read, hearing a text read aloud was how it became common knowledge. No part of the people was to depend on another part to know what God had said.

Moses is thinking of the children in particular. Verse 13 speaks of children ‘who do not know the law’. Each generation has to hear it for the first time. Faith is never more than one generation from being forgotten, and so the law is to be read again and again.
passages.later:
A written law was found in the temple in the time of King Josiah: “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 22:8). Many scholars identify that book with some form of Deuteronomy.

After the exile, Ezra the priest did what this passage commands, at the Feast of Tabernacles, with ‘men and women and all who could listen and understand’ (Nehemiah 8:2). “And all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law” (Nehemiah 8:3).

The first Christians kept the practice of reading Scripture aloud when they met. Paul tells Timothy, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13).
passages.asks: The law was to be read to everyone together, with the children listening. Ask when you last heard a long passage of Scripture read aloud, and whether the children you know have ever heard one. And ask what you assume the next generation knows about God that no one has actually told them.

passages.t: God tells Moses what will happen, and gives a song
passages.happening:
God calls Moses and Joshua to the Tent of Meeting, and appears there in a pillar of cloud (verses 14-15).

What he says is hard. “You will soon rest with your fathers, and these people will rise up and prostitute themselves with the foreign gods of the land they are entering. They will forsake Me and break the covenant I have made with them” (verse 16). In that day God's anger will burn, and he will hide his face from them, and many troubles will come (verses 17-18).

So God gives an instruction. “Now therefore, write down for yourselves this song and teach it to the Israelites; have them recite it, so that it may be a witness for Me against them” (verse 19). When trouble comes, ‘this song will testify against them, because it will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants’ (verse 21).

Moses writes the song that same day and teaches it (verse 22). And God commissions Joshua: “Be strong and courageous, for you will bring the Israelites into the land that I swore to give them, and I will be with you” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the saddest moments in the life of Moses. He is about to die, and God tells him that the people he gave his life to will turn away after he is gone.

The language of verse 16 is the language of a broken marriage. The prophets later used the same picture often. Israel's bond with God was meant to be as close and exclusive as a marriage, and the worship of other gods is described as unfaithfulness to a husband.

To ‘hide My face’ is a Hebrew way of speaking about the withdrawal of favor. The phrase describes God's response to a nation's settled idolatry. It is not a description of what is happening every time a believer feels that God is far away. The psalms are full of faithful people who cried out that God's face was hidden and who had done no such thing.

God says, ‘I know their inclination’. The Hebrew word means something formed or shaped. The same word is used in Genesis of the bent of the human heart.

And then God gives them a song. A scroll can be lost or left unread. A song learned in childhood stays. The people will carry in their own mouths the explanation of what has happened to them, so that when disaster comes they will not be able to say that no one told them. The song is called a witness against them. It is also a kindness. It ends, as the next chapter shows, with God's compassion on his people.

Joshua hears all of this. He is commissioned in the same breath as he learns that the people he is to lead will fail. He is told to be strong, and he is given one reason: ‘I will be with you’.
passages.later:
A psalm of the faithful asks the question of verse 17 from the other side: “Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?” (Psalm 44:24).

Paul took leave of the church at Ephesus as Moses takes leave of Israel here, knowing what would come: “I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock” (Acts 20:29).
passages.hard:
If God knew that Israel would turn away, why did he go on with the covenant?

The chapter does not hide the difficulty. God foretells unfaithfulness, and in the same hour brings Israel toward the land and binds them to himself.

Readers have answered in different ways. Some stress that knowing a thing beforehand does not cause it. Israel remains fully responsible, and the song is given so that no one can plead ignorance. Others stress that God's covenant rests on his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and not on Israel's performance, so that his commitment is not cancelled by their failure. Chapter 30 has already promised restoration on the far side of judgment.

Traditions that lay weight on God's rule over all things and traditions that lay weight on human freedom both find support here, and these notes take no side between them. Both agree on what the chapter shows. God stays with a people he knows will fail him, and that is grace.

These are words about Israel in its own Scriptures, spoken so that Israel would live. They give no one else a reason to look down on the Jewish people. The New Testament says the same kind of thing about the church.
passages.asks: God commissioned Joshua knowing what was coming, and gave him a promise and not a guarantee of success. Ask whether you are holding back from a task because you cannot be sure it will turn out well. And ask what you have learned by heart that would still be with you if everything else were taken.

passages.happening:
When Moses has finished writing the law in a book, ‘from beginning to end’, he gives it to the Levites who carry the ark. “Take this Book of the Law and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, so that it may remain there as a witness against you” (verse 26).

He speaks plainly to them. “For I know how rebellious and stiff-necked you are. If you are already rebelling against the LORD while I am still alive, how much more will you rebel after my death!” (verse 27).

He has the elders and officers gathered, to speak the words in their hearing and to ‘call heaven and earth to witness against them’ (verse 28). Then he recites the song to the whole assembly, from beginning to end (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The ark was the gold-covered chest that held the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. It stood in the inner room of the tabernacle. The written law is placed beside it. The tablets lie inside the ark, and the book lies at its side.

There are now two witnesses. One is the song, which the people will carry in their mouths. The other is the book, which lies in the holiest place. One is sung and one is written. Neither depends on anyone's memory of Moses.

Moses' words in verse 27 are blunt. He has known this people for forty years and has no illusions. It is the speech of a man who loves them and will not flatter them on his way out.

It should be heard as that. Moses is an Israelite speaking to Israelites. The Bible's sharpest words about Israel are spoken by Israel's own leaders and prophets, in love, and kept by Israel in its own Scriptures. They were never meant to be taken up by others as a verdict on the Jewish people.

The chapter ends in the middle of a sentence. It leads straight into the song.
passages.later:
King Josiah's reform began when this book, or one like it, was brought out and read, and ‘he tore his clothes’ (2 Kings 22:11).

Jesus said of the Scriptures of Moses that they still do what verse 26 says, and that they point to him: “If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me” (John 5:46).
passages.asks: Moses left Israel a book and a song, and not a successor who could replace him. Ask what will remain of what you have taught when you are no longer there to say it. And think of verse 27. Ask whether there is someone who loves you enough to tell you the truth about yourself, and whether you listen.
